title: Show a fraction of a region, of a set and of a length

lesson.title: One Fraction, Three Pictures

steps.say: You already know how to cut a whole into equal parts, and you know the bottom number counts all the equal parts while the top number counts the ones we mean. Today we do just one small thing with that: show the very same fraction, three fourths, in three different pictures — a shape, a group of things, and a length.

First, a fraction of a region. Picture a little blueberry pie cut into four equal slices. You eat three of them. The whole pie is four equal slices, and you took three, so you ate three fourths of the pie. Bottom number four, because the whole pie has four equal slices. Top number three, because three are yours.

visual.caption: A pie in 4 equal slices, 3 shaded — three fourths

steps.say: Now a fraction of a set. Here are eight blueberries, and I put them into four equal groups, two berries in each group. If three of those four groups go into your bowl, you have three fourths of the berries. Look at the groups, not the single berries — four groups in all, three groups taken. And it matches: three groups is six berries out of eight, which is the same as three fourths.

visual.caption: 8 berries in 4 equal groups of 2 — take 3 groups

steps.say: And now a fraction of a length. Here is a number line from zero to one, like one whole metre of ribbon cut into four equal pieces. Hop three pieces from zero and you land on three fourths. So three fourths of a metre is seventy five centimetres of ribbon — same fraction, just measured along a line.

visual.caption: 0 to 1 split into 4 equal jumps — the point sits at three fourths

steps.say: Here is the slip-up I want you to watch for with sets. Say you have six stickers and two of them are shiny. Some kids look at the two shiny ones, then look at the four plain ones, and write two fourths. That is not right — four is only the leftovers, not the whole set. The bottom number must count everything in the set, and there are six stickers altogether, so it is two sixths. Always ask yourself, how many are there in total?

visual.caption: 6 stickers in all: 2 shiny + 4 plain — the whole set is 6, so two sixths

steps.say: So remember: a fraction can be part of a shape, part of a group, or part of a length, and in every single one the bottom number is the whole thing.

lesson.answer: Shape, group, or length — the bottom number always counts the WHOLE, the top counts the part you mean.

practice.question: At a BC blueberry farm your family buys a pie and cuts it into eight equal slices. Your family eats five of those slices. Draw the pie yourself as a circle cut into eight equal pieces, shade five, and tell me what fraction of the pie was eaten.
practice.answer: Five eighths of the pie was eaten. The whole pie is eight equal slices, so eight is the bottom number, and five slices were eaten, so five is the top number. (Three eighths is still left over.)
